The September 30 GDP revision strengthens the US growth picture, but its 2.2% annualized headline runs below private domestic demand. Revisions and price measures explain the gap.

Original VJOURNAL reporting and analysis synthesized from the cited official releases, checked on 1 October 2026. Historical methodological sources are identified as context. The cover is an AI-generated conceptual illustration of a generic setting.

BEA raised second-quarter real GDP growth from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annual rate.

results.text:
Daily Risk Assessment October 4, 2026

# Recession Risk 34/100 — October 4, 2026

US recession risk over the next 90 days is MODERATE: the labor-market trigger most correlated with imminent recessions is not flashing (Sahm Rule remains well below the 0.50 trigger at ~0.07, and insured-unemployment-based signals remain low). The yield curve has re-steepened (2s10s around +35 to +45 bps), which historically reduces near-term recession odds versus an active inversion, and financial conditions remain loose (NFCI strongly negative, VIX low). Offsetting this, key cyclicals are deteriorating: temporary help employment is contracting (a classic early labor leading indicator), freight/goods activity is weak, and consumer psychology is very depressed even as equities remain near highs. Net: the data do not support an “imminent recession” call inside 90 days, but the balance of leading signals has shifted toward late-cycle slowing with downside tail risk rising.

The business activity index for the service sector fell 5.2 points in September to 56.5 after having risen 2 6 points in August. We tend to focus on the business activity component as a measure of “production” because it seems to track better with the pace of economic activity. Trump’s imposition of tariffs, federal government layoffs, and deportation of immigrants made people in the service sector nervous throughout 2025.
